organism: Measles virus, a paramyxovirus (genus Morbillivirus) with a single-stranded, negative-sense RNA genome. Its F (fusion) and H (hemagglutinin) envelope proteins drive host-cell entry. There is only one antigenic type - documented changes to the H protein have not translated into any observed loss of vaccine efficacy. The virus is rapidly inactivated by heat, sunlight, acidic pH, ether, and trypsin.
clinicalFeaturesSummary: Incubation to prodrome averages 11-12 days; exposure to rash onset averages 14 days (range 7-21). The 2-4 day prodrome brings a stepwise fever rising to 103F-105F, cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis. Koplik spots - blue-white spots on red buccal mucosa - are considered unique to measles and appear 1-2 days before the rash. The maculopapular rash starts at the hairline, spreads down and out to the hands and feet over about 3 days, lasts 5-6 days total, and fades in the same head-to-extremities order it appeared. About 30% of US cases (1987-2000) had a complication - diarrhea, otitis media, pneumonia, encephalitis, or subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) - most often in children under 5 and in adults.
epidemiologySummary: Measles is a human-only disease with no known animal reservoir and no documented asymptomatic carrier state. It spreads person-to-person via large respiratory droplets and via airborne aerosolized droplet nuclei that can remain infectious in a closed space for up to 2 hours after an infected person leaves. In endemic temperate areas it occurs mainly in late winter and spring. It is highly communicable - secondary attack rates exceed 90% among susceptible close contacts - and a case is considered contagious from 4 days before through 4 days after rash onset.
secularTrendsSummary: Before 1963, the US reported about 500,000 cases and 500 deaths annually (actual incidence was estimated at 3-4 million cases/year), with epidemics every 2-3 years and over 90% of people infected by age 15. Incidence fell more than 95% after vaccine licensure in 1963. Outbreaks among vaccinated school-age children in the 1980s (primary vaccine failure) led to the second-dose recommendation in 1989. The US declared indigenous transmission interrupted in 2000, but importation-driven outbreaks continue: 2019 saw 13 outbreaks and 663 cases, 88% of them in underimmunized close-knit communities. MMR coverage by 24 months was 90.7% for the 2016-2017 birth cohort.
vaccineDescription: MMR (MMR-II) and MMRV (ProQuad) are the only measles-containing vaccines used in the US - there is no single-antigen measles vaccine. Both are live, attenuated, lyophilized preparations reconstituted with sterile preservative-free water, given subcutaneously, and contain gelatin and neomycin with no adjuvant or preservative. MMRV's varicella component is higher-titer than the single-antigen varicella vaccine.
vaccinationScheduleSummary: Routine schedule is 2 doses: dose 1 at 12-15 months (minimum age 12 months), dose 2 at 4-6 years, with a minimum interval of 4 weeks between MMR doses (3 months for MMRV, though a 4-week interval is still considered valid). For the first dose in children 12-47 months, separate MMR and varicella vaccines are generally preferred over MMRV because MMRV roughly doubles the risk of febrile seizure at that age; MMRV is generally preferred for the second dose and for a first dose given at 48 months or older.
evidenceOfImmunitySummary: A person can generally be considered immune to measles without a documented vaccination if they were born before 1957, have serologic evidence of immunity (an equivocal test result counts as negative), have laboratory-confirmed disease, or have documentation of adequate vaccination. Health care personnel are held to a stricter standard - even those born before 1957 should have documented immunity, since serologic studies found 5%-10% of hospital personnel born before that year had no detectable antibody to measles, mumps, or rubella.
vaccineEfficacySummary: About 95% of children develop measles antibodies after a single dose at 12 months; more than 99% do after 2 doses. Vaccine-induced immunity appears long-term and probably lifelong in most people - those who appear to lose antibody usually show a rapid anamnestic response on revaccination, suggesting they remain immune. Waning immunity appears to occur only rarely and plays a minor role in transmission and outbreaks.
contraindicationsSummary: A severe allergic reaction to a vaccine component or a prior dose is a contraindication, as is severe immunocompromise (malignancy, chemotherapy, congenital immunodeficiency, long-term immunosuppressive therapy, or HIV with severe immunosuppression), high-dose systemic corticosteroid therapy for 14 or more days (wait at least 1 month after stopping), a family history of congenital or hereditary immunodeficiency in a first-degree relative (unless the recipient's own immunocompetence is verified), and pregnancy - pregnancy should be avoided for 4 weeks after vaccination, though inadvertent vaccination during pregnancy is not itself a reason to consider ending the pregnancy. MMRV additionally treats HIV infection, regardless of immune status, as a contraindication. Precautions include moderate/severe acute illness, alpha-gal allergy, recent receipt of antibody-containing blood products (wait 3-11 months before vaccinating), a history of thrombocytopenic purpura, and an upcoming TB skin test. Egg allergy is explicitly not a reason for special precautions - MMR may be given without prior skin testing.
vaccineSafetySummary: 5%-15% of susceptible MMR recipients develop a fever of 103F or higher, usually 7-12 days after vaccination; about 5% get a transient rash around 7-10 days post-vaccination. Febrile seizures occur in roughly 1 per 3,000-4,000 MMR doses. MMRV carries a higher first-dose risk in children 12-23 months (about 1 additional febrile seizure per 2,300-2,600 children compared with separate MMR and varicella vaccines) - an effect not seen for the second dose or in children 4-6 years old. Anaphylaxis occurs in 1.8-14.4 cases per million doses. Arthralgia and other joint symptoms (attributed to the rubella component) occur in up to 25% of adult women. Multiple studies and a National Academy of Medicine review have found no causal link between MMR and autism or inflammatory bowel disease.
vaccineStorageSummary: Follow manufacturer guidance for MMR-II and ProQuad specifically; see CDC's Vaccine Storage and Handling Toolkit for general best practices.
surveillanceSummary: Laboratory confirmation typically relies on RT-PCR (nasopharyngeal aspirate, throat swab, or urine) and/or measles-specific IgM serology; testing can also distinguish recent vaccine virus from wild-type virus in a potentially exposed, recently vaccinated person. See CDC's Manual for the Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases for state/local reporting guidance.

supplementalTopics.title: Vaccination of Adults and Healthcare Personnel
supplementalTopics.summary: Adults born in 1957 or later need at least 1 documented MMR dose or other acceptable evidence of immunity. Students entering college or other post-high-school institutions should have 2 documented doses before enrollment. Health care personnel need 2 doses for measles/mumps immunity and 1 dose for rubella immunity - including those born before 1957 - and facilities should offer an additional outbreak-specific dose to personnel during a measles or mumps outbreak (2 doses) or rubella outbreak (1 dose).

supplementalTopics.title: International Travel
supplementalTopics.summary: Because measles remains endemic or epidemic in much of the world, travelers should have documented immunity before departure: 1 dose of MMR for infants age 6 through 11 months, and 2 age-appropriate doses of MMR or MMRV for children 12 months and older and for adults.

supplementalTopics.title: Revaccination After an Invalid Prior Dose
supplementalTopics.summary: Several groups should be treated as unvaccinated and given a fresh 2-dose series: people vaccinated before their first birthday, those who received a killed-virus vaccine, those vaccinated 1963-1967 with an unknown vaccine type, those who received immune globulin alongside an older attenuated-strain vaccine, and people with perinatal HIV infection who were vaccinated before effective antiretroviral therapy was established and lack evidence of current severe immunosuppression. A dose given before 12 months of age (e.g. for early international travel) does not count toward the routine 2-dose series.

keyPoints: First live attenuated measles vaccine licensed 1963; MMR licensed 1971; MMRV licensed 2005
Before vaccination, infection was nearly universal in childhood; still common and often fatal in developing countries (WHO estimated 142,300 global deaths in 2018)
Koplik spots (blue-white spots on red buccal mucosa) are considered unique to measles and appear just before the rash
Airborne transmission: infectious droplet nuclei can linger in a closed room for up to 2 hours after an infected person leaves
Contagious from 4 days before through 4 days after rash onset
Birth before 1957 is generally accepted as evidence of immunity, except for health care personnel, who need documented immunity regardless of birth year
No causal link to autism or inflammatory bowel disease, per multiple studies and a National Academy of Medicine review
